body:
Why different battery technologies are being developed

No single battery chemistry satisfies every requirement equally well. A mobile phone benefits from compact storage, whereas a large electricity network may place greater importance on cost, long operating life and the ability to store energy for several hours.

Different battery technologies therefore use different electrode materials, electrolytes and arrangements. Three important categories are sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries and flow batteries.

These categories are not defined using the same criterion. Sodium-ion identifies the principal mobile ion. Solid-state identifies the physical nature of the electrolyte. Flow battery identifies the way electrochemically active materials are stored and circulated.

Sodium-ion batteries

A sodium-ion battery operates through the reversible movement of sodium ions between suitable electrodes, following a broad electrochemical principle similar to that of lithium-ion batteries.

Sodium is more abundant in nature than lithium. This creates an opportunity to develop battery chemistries with reduced dependence on lithium and potentially lower material costs.

However, sodium-ion batteries require electrode materials compatible with sodium-ion movement. Hard carbon is an important negative-electrode material for many sodium-ion designs.

Typical commercial sodium-ion batteries generally have lower energy density than leading high-energy lithium-ion batteries, although performance varies by chemistry and development stage. They are of interest for stationary storage and for applications where low cost and material availability matter more than achieving the highest possible energy density.

Sodium-ion technology does not automatically eliminate dependence on every critical material. Its supply requirements depend on the particular cathode, negative electrode and other cell components.

Sodium-ion: Sodium ions are the charge-carrying species.
Lithium-ion: Lithium ions are the charge-carrying species.
Both remain electrochemical rechargeable-battery families.

Solid-state batteries

In a conventional lithium-ion battery, the electrolyte commonly contains a liquid medium. A solid-state battery uses a solid material to conduct ions between the electrodes.

The solid electrolyte performs the required internal ion-transport function while remaining physically solid.

Solid electrolytes may be ceramic, polymer-based or other suitable solid ion-conducting materials. Some solid-state designs aim to improve energy density, safety or durability, but actual results depend on the complete system.

Using a solid electrolyte can reduce certain risks associated with flammable liquid electrolytes. Nevertheless, solid-state batteries are not automatically free from short circuits, overheating or other safety problems.

Solid-state is not a synonym for lithium-ion. A solid-state battery may use lithium-based or another suitable electrochemical system.

Flow batteries

A redox flow battery stores energy in electrochemically active substances, usually dissolved in liquids held in external storage tanks.

During operation, the liquids circulate through an electrochemical cell, where oxidation and reduction reactions permit electrical energy to be absorbed or released.

A typical flow system contains 2 electrolyte reservoirs, pumps, a central electrochemical cell and a separator or membrane that allows suitable ions to pass between the cell compartments.

Why flow batteries are useful for stationary storage

In a flow battery, the amount of energy that can be stored depends strongly on the quantity and nature of the active electrolyte. The system's power capability depends strongly on the electrochemical cell arrangement.

This makes it possible to increase stored-energy capacity by increasing the appropriate electrolyte-storage capacity without increasing the power capability in exactly the same proportion.

Flow batteries are therefore of interest for electricity-network storage, particularly where longer discharge duration is valuable. However, their tanks, pumps and circulation systems take up space and add cost and operational requirements.

Vanadium redox flow batteries are a well-known example. Vanadium can exist in different oxidation states, allowing vanadium-containing electrolytes to participate in reversible electrochemical reactions.

Comparing the technologies correctly

TechnologyDefining featureImportant consideration
Lithium-ionLithium ions move between electrodesWidely used; performance depends on chemistry
Sodium-ionSodium ions move between electrodesAbundant sodium; energy-density trade-offs
Solid-stateSolid electrolyte conducts ionsPotential benefits depend on the full design
FlowActive liquid electrolytes circulate through a cellExternal tanks make stationary energy storage flexible

These labels are not mutually exclusive in the same way. A lithium-based battery can have a solid electrolyte. The term solid-state describes the electrolyte, whereas lithium-ion describes the mobile ion.

Choosing a battery for an application

A suitable energy-storage technology is selected according to several considerations: stored energy, required power, available space, expected cycle life, safety, cost, material availability and operating conditions.

For instance, a lightweight electric vehicle may prioritise energy density, while a stationary facility with adequate space may be able to use a bulkier storage system designed for longer discharge duration.

Prelims focus

  • Sodium-ion batteries use sodium ions rather than lithium ions as the principal moving charge carriers.
  • Hard carbon is an important negative-electrode material for many sodium-ion designs.
  • Solid-state batteries are defined by the use of a solid electrolyte.
  • Flow batteries use circulating electrochemically active liquids stored in external tanks.
  • Vanadium is used in an important family of redox flow batteries.
  • Flow batteries can scale stored energy and power capability with greater independence than many conventional sealed-cell systems.
  • Trap: Sodium-ion and solid-state describe different characteristics and should not be treated as mutually exclusive categories.

[Argonne National Laboratory, Argonne Researchers Crack a Key Problem with Sodium-Ion Batteries for Electric Vehicles and Grid Energy Storage, consulted 14 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Project Selections for Critical Material Innovation, Efficiency, and Alternatives, Set 2, sodium-ion and hard-carbon materials, consulted 14 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Hops and Jumps Help Lithium Ions Flow Faster in a Solid-State Battery Material, 23 September 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, New Report Showcases How Innovation Can Fast Track Affordable Energy Storage, flow-battery description, consulted 14 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Flow Battery Solution for Smart Grid Renewable Energy Applications, 28 August 2017.]

title: Sodium-Ion, Solid-State and Flow Batteries: Comparing Emerging Storage Systems

body:
Why battery materials are strategically important

A battery is not made from a single mineral. Its performance depends on several materials used in the electrodes, electrolyte, separator, current collectors and protective components.

The rapid development of electric transport and electricity storage increases the importance of reliable access to these materials.

In lithium-ion systems, commonly relevant materials include lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, manganese, iron, copper and aluminium. Their roles and quantities vary with battery chemistry.

Different chemistries need different materials

Battery component or chemistryRelevant materialsKey distinction
Common lithium-ion negative electrodeGraphiteStores lithium during charging
LFP positive electrodeLithium, iron, phosphateNo nickel or cobalt required in this cathode
NMC positive electrodeLithium, nickel, manganese, cobaltRequires nickel and cobalt
Many sodium-ion negative electrodesHard carbonCompatible with sodium-ion storage

Using a chemistry that avoids cobalt or nickel can change supply-chain requirements. It does not remove the need for other materials, energy, processing or manufacturing.

What makes a mineral critical?

A mineral is considered critical in a particular policy or economic context when it is important for significant activities and its supply may be vulnerable to disruption.

Supply risk can arise from the geographic concentration of mining, limited processing capacity, trade restrictions, environmental constraints or difficulties in obtaining suitable material quality.

The existence of a mineral deposit does not automatically mean that battery-grade material is immediately available. Mining, refining, chemical processing and manufacturing are separate parts of the supply chain.

Environmental and social considerations

Mining and processing can require land, water and energy and may create pollution if not properly controlled. Manufacturing and transporting batteries also have environmental impacts.

Battery technologies can contribute to cleaner energy systems, especially when charged using low-emission electricity, but their complete environmental impact must consider raw-material extraction, production, operation and end-of-life management.

Changing battery chemistry, improving durability and recovering materials after use can reduce some supply and environmental pressures. The extent of the benefit depends on actual processes and operating conditions.

Reuse, refurbishment and recycling

These terms describe different activities and should not be confused.

  • Reuse: A suitable battery or component is used again without fundamentally converting it into raw materials.
  • Refurbishment: A battery or battery system is repaired, restored or otherwise made suitable for further service where technically and safely appropriate.
  • Recycling: Waste batteries are processed to recover materials that can be used again in manufacturing or other applications.

Some electric-vehicle batteries may remain suitable for selected less demanding applications after their original use. Such second-life use requires appropriate assessment; it is not safe or economical for every battery.

How battery recycling works

Used batteries should enter appropriate collection and recycling channels because they may retain electrical energy and contain hazardous or reactive substances.

At a broad level, recycling involves collection, safe handling, separation of components and recovery of useful materials.

Two important recovery approaches are:

  • Pyrometallurgy: Uses high-temperature processing to recover selected valuable materials.
  • Hydrometallurgy: Uses liquid-based chemical processes to separate and recover selected materials.

The materials recovered and the efficiency of recovery depend on the battery chemistry and the particular recycling process. Recycling does not necessarily recover every substance or return every material directly to battery-grade quality.

Why recycling matters for supply security

Recovered materials can provide an additional source of battery inputs. This may reduce the need for some newly extracted resources and help diversify supply.

However, recycling alone cannot immediately meet all demand for new batteries, especially when the total number of batteries in use is expanding. A combination of efficient material use, appropriate chemistries, reliable sourcing, longer product life and recycling is necessary.

Prelims focus

  • Battery material requirements vary by electrode chemistry.
  • Graphite is a common negative-electrode material in lithium-ion batteries.
  • LFP cathodes avoid nickel and cobalt; NMC cathodes contain them.
  • A critical mineral combines strategic importance with possible supply vulnerability in the relevant policy context.
  • Reuse, refurbishment and recycling are different activities.
  • Pyrometallurgy uses high temperatures; hydrometallurgy uses liquid-based chemical processes.
  • Trap: Recycling does not guarantee complete recovery of all materials or remove every need for fresh mineral production.

[U.S. Department of Energy, Reducing Reliance on Cobalt for Lithium-ion Batteries, cathode materials and supply dependence, consulted 14 November 2026; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Lithium-Ion Battery Recycling and Lithium-Ion Battery Recycling Frequently Asked Questions, recovery methods and safe handling, consulted 14 November 2026; Government of India, Ministry of Mines, Strategic Supply Chain Management for Critical Minerals, 24 March 2025.]
